metadata.summary: This guideline addresses the diagnosis, classification, treatment, and follow-up of dry eye syndrome, including aqueous tear deficiency and evaporative dry eye. It describes clinical examination and diagnostic testing, a staged range of medical and procedural treatments, and care around cataract and refractive surgery. Its appendices also address Sjögren’s syndrome and neuropathic ocular pain.

care_settings: Preoperative and postoperative care for cataract and lens-based surgery
Preoperative and postoperative care for keratorefractive surgery
target_population: Individuals of all ages with symptoms and signs suggestive of dry eye
Patients with dry eye considering cataract, lens-based, or keratorefractive surgery
Patients with dry eye and suspected or established systemic disease
Children with possible dry eye disease
therapeutic_areas: Patient education and modification of environmental and contributing factors
Moisture chamber spectacles and overnight treatments
Autologous/allogeneic serum eye drops and other blood-based products
Surgical approaches for severe dry eye

toxicities.event: Ocular surface injury associated with frequently instilled preserved eye drops
prevention: Nonpreserved tear substitutes are generally recommended when substitutes are used frequently and chronically, for example, more than four times a day.
Nonpreserved ocular lubricants may be considered to limit preservative-related toxicity.

toxicities.event: Transient visual blurring with viscous ocular lubricants
recognition: Blurred vision associated with more viscous preparations

toxicities.incidence: Ocular burning was reported in 17% of patients.

toxicities.event: Increased intraocular pressure and cataract formation during topical corticosteroid treatment
prevention: Monitor patients prescribed topical corticosteroids for these adverse effects.
Low-dose topical corticosteroids can be given intermittently for short periods, such as several weeks, to suppress ocular surface inflammation.

toxicities.event: Irritation, epiphora, extrusion and canalicular stenosis associated with silicone punctal plugs
toxicities.incidence: In one study, 56% of silicone plugs remained in place after 2 years; among patients whose plugs were lost spontaneously, 34% had canalicular stenosis at 2 years.
recognition: Conjunctival irritation related to plug shape or position

management.actions: A silicone plug can be removed.

management.severity: Spontaneous plug loss in a patient who benefited from occlusion
management.actions: The plug can be replaced, or the punctum can be closed permanently by thermal cautery or another method.

prevention: Use the largest plug that can be inserted to reduce extrusion.

toxicities.event: Epiphora and infection-related complications associated with punctal plugs
recognition: Blockage with secondary infection after displacement of a plug into the lacrimal system

management.severity: Displaced plug within the lacrimal system
management.actions: Surgical removal is rarely needed; a displaced plug may pass through the drainage system.

prevention: Before planned punctal cautery, generally perform a trial with nonpermanent implants to assess the potential for epiphora; silicone punctal plugs are more useful for this purpose.

toxicities.event: Infection risk with therapeutic contact lenses
recognition: Contact lens intolerance in severe dry eye
Infection risk in associated neurotrophic keratopathy or with extended soft-lens wear
prevention: Use contact lenses cautiously when neurotrophic keratopathy accompanies dry eye.
Consider the additional infection risk, particularly with extended wear of soft contact lenses.

toxicities.event: Excessive sweating and other drug-related adverse effects with oral pilocarpine
toxicities.incidence: Excessive sweating occurred in over 40% of patients. Two percent of patients taking oral pilocarpine withdrew from the study because of sweating and other drug-related adverse effects.

toxicities.event: Ocular irritation from rose bengal dye
prevention: Inform patients that the dye may irritate the eye; topical anesthetic is typically used before instillation.

toxicities.event: Worsening dry eye symptoms after keratorefractive or lens-based surgery
toxicities.incidence: Dry eye symptoms persisting beyond the normal postoperative period of 3 months occur in about one third of individuals.
recognition: Dry eye symptoms during the first few months after surgery
prevention: Counsel patients considering keratorefractive or lens-based surgery that dry eye symptoms may worsen.
Improving pre-existing contributors to dry eye before surgery can reduce the likelihood of worsening.
Evaluate and manage dry eye before and after lens-based surgery in all patients undergoing that surgery.
Achieve effective dry eye treatment before keratorefractive surgery; uncontrolled dry eye syndrome is a contraindication to that surgery.

prophylaxis.recommendation: Generally use nonpreserved tear substitutes when tear substitutes are instilled frequently and chronically to limit preservative-related ocular surface toxicity.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients using tear substitutes frequently and chronically, for example, more than four times a day.

prophylaxis.recommendation: Monitor for increased intraocular pressure and cataract formation during topical corticosteroid treatment for dry eye.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients prescribed topical corticosteroids for dry eye.

prophylaxis.recommendation: Before planned permanent punctal cautery, generally test nonpermanent occlusion for potential epiphora; a staged approach generally limits cautery to no more than one punctum in each eye per treatment session.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients with severe dry eye for whom punctal cautery is planned.

prophylaxis.recommendation: Assess and manage dry eye both before and after lens-based surgery, and improve pre-existing contributing factors where possible to reduce postoperative worsening.
Treat dry eye effectively before keratorefractive surgery; do not perform it when dry eye syndrome is uncontrolled.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients with dry eye considering keratorefractive surgery.

infection_management.pathogen_or_syndrome: Secondary infection following displacement of a punctal plug into the lacrimal system
infection_management.management: A displaced plug may pass through the lacrimal system; surgical removal is rarely necessary.

infection_management.pathogen_or_syndrome: Canaliculitis, dacryocystitis or keratitis associated with thermal labile polymer plugs
Infection associated with therapeutic contact lens use
infection_management.prevention: Use contact lenses cautiously in patients with associated neurotrophic keratopathy and consider the additional infection risk, especially with extended soft-lens wear.

therapies_index.name: Patient education
therapies_index.administration: Discuss the chronic course, prognosis, treatment goals, aggravating factors, and practical use of prescribed therapies.
monitoring: Periodically reassess the patient's understanding and adherence.

therapies_index.name: Modification of local environment
therapies_index.administration: Measures discussed include increasing ambient humidity, avoiding drafts, altering airflow, positioning a computer screen below eye level, taking regular breaks, and consciously blinking fully.

therapies_index.name: Modification/elimination of offending systemic and topical medications
therapies_index.administration: Identify medicines that may aggravate dry eye and consider changing or eliminating them when feasible.

therapies_index.name: Oral essential fatty acid supplementation
therapies_index.administration: Oral supplementation is listed among potential dietary changes. A cited study found no benefit over placebo during 12 months in moderate to severe dry eye; other reports described some improvement with adjunctive omega-3 supplements in blepharitis.

therapies_index.name: Ocular lubricants
therapies_index.administration: Topical preparations include artificial tears, emulsions, gels, and ointments. Lipid-containing supplements may be considered when MGD is present; thicker preparations may last longer but may blur vision.
key_toxicities: Frequently applied preserved eye drops may contribute to corneal epithelial damage and dry eye symptoms.

therapies_index.name: Nonpreserved ocular lubricants
therapies_index.administration: Generally recommended when tear substitutes are used chronically and frequently, for example, more than four times a day.

therapies_index.name: Eyelid hygiene
therapies_index.administration: Various approaches to eyelid hygiene are listed as an initial management option.

therapies_index.name: Tea tree oil
therapies_index.administration: Listed as a treatment option when Demodex is present.

therapies_index.name: lotilaner
therapies_index.administration: Eye drops are listed as a treatment option when Demodex is present.

therapies_index.name: ivermectin 1% cream
therapies_index.administration: The guide lists off-label cream use for Demodex.

therapies_index.name: Punctal occlusion
therapies_index.mechanism: Reduces tear drainage to conserve tears on the ocular surface.
therapies_index.administration: Consider for aqueous tear deficiency when medical approaches to increasing tear volume are ineffective or impractical; plugs are preferably placed after tear homeostasis is achieved.

therapies_index.name: Silicone plugs
therapies_index.mechanism: Occlude a punctum to conserve tears.
therapies_index.administration: Place an appropriately sized plug in the punctum; the guide favors the largest size that can be inserted to lower the chance of extrusion. The plug can be removed if irritation or epiphora develops.
key_toxicities: Conjunctival irritation related to plug shape or position
Canalicular stenosis reported after spontaneous loss
A plug displaced into the lacrimal system may cause obstruction with secondary infection
monitoring: Assess retention, irritation, and symptoms of epiphora.

therapies_index.name: Collagen plugs
therapies_index.mechanism: Occlude a punctum to conserve tears.
therapies_index.administration: Listed as a material for punctal occlusion.

therapies_index.name: Thermal labile polymer plugs
therapies_index.administration: Placed within the canaliculus rather than at the ocular surface.

therapies_index.name: Moisture chamber spectacles/goggles
therapies_index.administration: Listed for tear conservation, including use during activities associated with visual effort and as an overnight option.

therapies_index.name: Eyeglass side shields
therapies_index.administration: May be used to limit exposure to air drafts.

therapies_index.name: Overnight treatments
therapies_index.administration: Options named are ointment or moisture chamber devices.

therapies_index.name: In-office, physical heating and expression of the meibomian glands
therapies_index.administration: Performed in the office; thermal pulsation devices are included among the options.

therapies_index.name: Topical antibiotic
therapies_index.administration: Short-term application to the eyelid margins is listed for anterior blepharitis when present.

therapies_index.name: Oral macrolide or tetracycline antibiotics
therapies_index.administration: Listed among prescription options in the staged dry eye management approach; no specific agent or dose is given.

therapies_index.name: cyclosporine
therapies_index.mechanism: Prevents activation and nuclear translocation of transcription factors needed for T-cell activation and inflammatory cytokine production; it also inhibits mitochondrial pathways involved in apoptosis.
approved_indications: FDA-approved treatment for dry eye syndrome
therapies_index.administration: Topical formulations are described at 0.05% and 0.09%. After 1 full year of twice-daily treatment, the dose can be reduced to once a day in some patients without loss of benefit.
key_toxicities: Ocular burning, reported in 17% of patients in a cited study

therapies_index.name: lifitegrast
therapies_index.mechanism: The precise mechanism in dry eye is unknown. A proposed action is interruption of the interaction between LFA-1 and ICAM-1, which contributes to T-cell activation and migration.
approved_indications: FDA-approved treatment of signs and symptoms of dry eye syndrome
therapies_index.administration: Topical ophthalmic solution. The highlighted findings list lifitegrast 0.5%, whereas the management discussion identifies the FDA-approved solution and studied treatment as lifitegrast 5%; the guide does not resolve this discrepancy.

therapies_index.name: loteprednol etabonate 0.25%
approved_indications: FDA-approved treatment for dry eye syndrome
therapies_index.administration: Topical use for 2 weeks was studied; extending treatment to 4 weeks produced no additional benefit in the cited study.
key_toxicities: Potential increased intraocular pressure with topical corticosteroid treatment
Potential cataract formation with topical corticosteroid treatment
monitoring: Monitor patients receiving topical corticosteroids for increased intraocular pressure and cataract formation.

therapies_index.name: Topical corticosteroid
therapies_index.administration: The guide describes low-dose treatment at infrequent intervals for short periods, such as several weeks; longer treatment is listed as a later-stage option. Short-term application to the eyelid margins is also listed when anterior blepharitis is present.
monitoring: Monitor for increased intraocular pressure and cataract formation.

therapies_index.name: Topical secretagogues
therapies_index.administration: Listed among prescription treatment options without a named agent or dosing schedule.

therapies_index.name: varenicline
therapies_index.mechanism: Activates nicotinic acetylcholine receptors in the nasal trigeminal pathway, stimulating the lacrimal functional unit and tear film production.
approved_indications: FDA-approved treatment of signs and symptoms of dry eye syndrome
therapies_index.administration: Aqueous nasal spray; no dosing schedule is specified.

therapies_index.name: perfluorohexyloctane
approved_indications: FDA-approved management of signs and symptoms of dry eye
therapies_index.administration: A nonaqueous, preservative-free ophthalmic drop. In a cited trial involving dry eye secondary to meibomian gland dysfunction, drops were administered four times daily for 2 months.

therapies_index.name: Slow-release hydroxypropyl cellulose inserts
therapies_index.administration: Ocular inserts are described as occasionally helpful when a patient cannot apply artificial tears.

therapies_index.name: Oral secretagogues
therapies_index.mechanism: The oral cholinergic agents discussed stimulate glandular secretion through muscarinic receptors and may improve tear production.
therapies_index.administration: Listed as a later-stage option; the guide discusses use particularly when dry eye and dry mouth coexist.

therapies_index.name: cevimeline
therapies_index.mechanism: Binds muscarinic receptors to stimulate salivary and sweat gland secretion and appears to increase tear production.
approved_indications: FDA-approved treatment of dry mouth symptoms in patients with Sjögren’s syndrome
therapies_index.administration: Oral; no dose is specified.

therapies_index.name: pilocarpine
therapies_index.mechanism: Binds muscarinic receptors to stimulate glandular secretion; its effect on pupil size may account for improvement in some visual symptoms.
therapies_index.administration: A cited study administered 5 mg orally four times a day to patients with Sjogren syndrome.
key_toxicities: Excessive sweating occurred in over 40% of patients in the cited study; 2% withdrew because of sweating and other drug-related adverse effects.

therapies_index.name: Autologous serum eye drops
therapies_index.administration: Topical blood-derived drops are listed for later-stage dry eye care. A cited systematic review assessed 20% autologous serum against artificial tears over 2 weeks.

therapies_index.name: Allogeneic serum eye drops
therapies_index.administration: Presented as an alternative when repeated blood sampling from the patient is not possible.

therapies_index.name: Autologous plasma rich in growth factors drops
therapies_index.administration: Topical drops are discussed for severe dry eye, including in patients with Sjögren’s syndrome or GVHD.

therapies_index.name: Platelet-rich plasma eye drops
therapies_index.administration: Listed as a later-stage dry eye treatment option.

therapies_index.name: Blood based products
therapies_index.administration: Listed as a later-stage treatment category without further specification in the staged approach.

therapies_index.name: Soft bandage lenses
therapies_index.administration: A therapeutic contact lens option to use with caution. Soft contact lenses may help prevent recurrence of filamentary keratitis or relieve symptoms in selected cases.
key_toxicities: Poor tolerance in severe dry eye
Infection risk, particularly with extended wear and when neurotrophic keratopathy is also present

therapies_index.name: Rigid scleral lenses
therapies_index.administration: A therapeutic contact lens option discussed for severe dry eye; fitting, cost, and the patient's ability to insert and remove lenses may limit use.

therapies_index.name: Amniotic membrane grafts
therapies_index.administration: Listed as a later-stage option. Self-retaining or sutureless amniotic membrane may be considered for refractory filamentary keratitis, with recognition that its effect is short term.

therapies_index.name: Surgical punctal occlusion (punctal cautery)
therapies_index.mechanism: Permanently closes a punctum to conserve tears.
therapies_index.administration: Thermal or laser cautery may be used. The guide generally advises a prior trial with nonpermanent occlusion to assess possible epiphora and a stepwise approach involving no more than one punctum in each eye per treatment session.
monitoring: Assess for epiphora during trial occlusion before cautery.

therapies_index.name: tarsorrhaphy
therapies_index.mechanism: A limited tarsorrhaphy can reduce tear film instability.
therapies_index.administration: May be performed in severe dry eye that has not responded to other therapies.

therapies_index.name: minor salivary gland transplantation
therapies_index.administration: Listed among later-stage surgical options; the guide reports favorable results for minor salivary gland transplantation in patients with SJS and ocular cicatricial pemphigoid.

therapies_index.name: labial/buccal mucous membrane transplantation
therapies_index.administration: Discussed among other available therapies with reported favorable results in patients with SJS and ocular cicatricial pemphigoid.

therapies_index.name: Filament debridement
therapies_index.administration: Filaments may be removed with a moistened cotton-tip applicator, a dry cellulose sponge, or forceps when filamentary keratitis accompanies severe dry eye.

therapies_index.name: N-acetylcysteine 10%
therapies_index.mechanism: As a topical mucolytic agent, decreases the viscosity of the mucinous tear film.
therapies_index.administration: Topical application is discussed for filamentary keratitis.

therapies_index.name: autologous serum tears
therapies_index.mechanism: Described as a topical nerve-regenerative therapy for peripheral neuropathic ocular pain.
therapies_index.administration: Topical use is discussed for peripheral NOP or corneal neuropathic pain.

therapies_index.name: pregabalin
therapies_index.administration: An oral neuromodulator discussed for pain with a central component or systemic comorbidities; agents may be used alone or in combination. The guide states that neuromodulators may require about 3 to 4 months at a therapeutic dose before pain decreases.

therapies_index.name: gabapentin
therapies_index.administration: An oral neuromodulator discussed for pain with a central component or systemic comorbidities; agents may be used alone or in combination. The guide states that neuromodulators may require about 3 to 4 months at a therapeutic dose before pain decreases.

therapies_index.name: duloxetine
therapies_index.administration: An oral neuromodulator discussed for pain with a central component or systemic comorbidities; agents may be used alone or in combination. The guide states that neuromodulators may require about 3 to 4 months at a therapeutic dose before pain decreases.

therapies_index.name: amitriptyline
therapies_index.administration: An oral neuromodulator discussed for pain with a central component or systemic comorbidities; agents may be used alone or in combination. The guide states that neuromodulators may require about 3 to 4 months at a therapeutic dose before pain decreases.

therapies_index.name: nortriptyline
therapies_index.administration: An oral neuromodulator discussed for pain with a central component or systemic comorbidities; agents may be used alone or in combination. The guide states that neuromodulators may require about 3 to 4 months at a therapeutic dose before pain decreases.

therapies_index.name: low-dose naltrexone
therapies_index.administration: An oral neuromodulator discussed for pain with a central component or systemic comorbidities; agents may be used alone or in combination. The guide states that neuromodulators may require about 3 to 4 months at a therapeutic dose before pain decreases.

therapies_index.name: transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation device
therapies_index.administration: May be considered as an adjunctive migraine-directed strategy when neuropathic ocular pain involves light sensitivity and headache.

therapies_index.name: botulinum toxin A
therapies_index.administration: Periorbital injections may be considered as an adjunctive migraine-directed strategy for light sensitivity and headache accompanying neuropathic ocular pain.

therapies_index.name: Periocular nerve blocks
therapies_index.administration: A periocular block containing a corticosteroid and a long-acting sodium channel blocker is discussed for cutaneous allodynia around the eye or postsurgical pain.

therapies_index.name: acupuncture
therapies_index.administration: May be considered as a complementary approach for neuropathic ocular pain.

therapies_index.name: cognitive behavioral therapy
therapies_index.administration: May be considered as a complementary approach for neuropathic ocular pain.

therapies_index.name: hypnosis
therapies_index.administration: May be considered as a complementary approach for neuropathic ocular pain.

therapies_index.name: hydroxychloroquine
therapies_index.administration: The guide notes its common oral use for fatigue and arthralgias in Sjögren’s syndrome, while stating that the literature does not provide strong evidence of efficacy for dry eye.

therapies_index.name: Anti-tumor necrosis factor agents
therapies_index.administration: Mentioned in a review of Sjögren-related sicca treatments as not found effective.

therapies_index.name: rituximab
therapies_index.administration: Mentioned in a review of Sjögren-related sicca treatments; evidence supporting efficacy was not strong.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with dry eye symptoms or mild disease; a trial of artificial tears is appropriate when symptoms suggest dry eye but examination shows no signs and other causes of irritation have been excluded.
decision_rules: Identify and address treatable contributors rather than relying on tear replacement alone.
Select treatments according to the patient's causes, severity, preferences, and response; options within a management step can be used together, and a treatment from another step may be appropriate.
If symptoms persist despite initial measures, consider the next management step.

recommended_regimens.name: Patient education
recommended_regimens.summary: Explain the chronic course, prognosis, treatment goals, and practical use of the treatment plan.

recommended_regimens.name: Environmental and behavioral modification
recommended_regimens.summary: Address low humidity, drafts, smoke exposure, and prolonged screen or reading activities. Options include humidifying the air, altering airflow, using spectacle side shields, positioning a computer screen below eye level, taking regular breaks, and blinking fully.

recommended_regimens.name: Modification of contributing medications
recommended_regimens.summary: Identify systemic and topical medications that may aggravate dryness and consider modifying or eliminating them when feasible.

recommended_regimens.name: Ocular lubricants
recommended_regimens.summary: Use artificial tears or other suitable lubricants. Preserved substitutes may suffice in mild disease with an otherwise healthy ocular surface; nonpreserved substitutes are generally recommended when use is frequent and chronic.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: A systematic literature review found artificial tears safe and effective, while noting substantial differences in study design and reporting across comparisons.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: For frequent, chronic use, the example threshold is more than four times a day.

recommended_regimens.name: Eyelid hygiene and warm compresses
recommended_regimens.summary: Use eyelid hygiene measures and warm compresses as initial treatment, particularly when eyelid disease contributes to symptoms.

alternative_regimens.name: Oral essential fatty acid supplementation
alternative_regimens.summary: Discuss as a possible dietary modification, without presenting it as an established substitute for other treatment.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Consider in light of the conflicting evidence described for oral fatty acid supplements.

alternative_regimens.name: Moisture chamber goggles
alternative_regimens.summary: May lessen discomfort associated with computer or reading activities.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Consider when exposure or sustained visual tasks aggravate symptoms.

response_assessment.timepoint: At follow-up intervals determined by severity, treatment, and response
response_assessment.method: Review symptoms, visual function, treatment use, and the ocular surface.
response_assessment.interpretation: Use the response and any ocular surface damage to adjust treatment.

supportive_care: Reassess the patient's understanding of the condition, adherence, treatment benefits, and possible complications.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: More viscous lubricants may last longer and require fewer applications but can blur vision. The practicality of frequent instillation depends in part on lifestyle and manual dexterity.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients whose initial management is inadequate, including patients with moderate dry eye.
decision_rules: Continue appropriate initial measures while adding treatments directed at tear preservation, ocular surface inflammation, or contributing eyelid disease.
Choose prescription treatment according to the individual presentation and the evidence for its specific indication; the listed medicines have differing mechanisms.

recommended_regimens.name: Nonpreserved ocular lubricants
recommended_regimens.summary: Use to reduce exposure to preservative-related toxicity when initial lubrication is inadequate.

recommended_regimens.name: Overnight ointment or moisture chamber devices
recommended_regimens.summary: Consider overnight protection as an additional tear-conserving measure.

recommended_regimens.name: Moisture chamber spectacles/goggles
recommended_regimens.summary: Consider reducing tear exposure with moisture-retaining eyewear.

recommended_regimens.name: Topical cyclosporine 0.05%
recommended_regimens.summary: Consider topical anti-inflammatory treatment when ocular inflammation contributes to dry eye. The guide describes both favorable individual studies and inconsistent findings in a subsequent review.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: In one study, a 10-mm increase in Schirmer test results compared with vehicle at 6 months occurred in 15% of cyclosporine-treated patients versus 5% of vehicle-treated patients. Another study reported success in 74%, 72%, and 67% of patients with mild, moderate, and severe dry eyes, respectively. A 2019 review of 30 randomized controlled trials (4,009 participants) found inconsistent evidence for effects on ocular discomfort, fluorescein staining, Schirmer test results, and TBUT.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: In a portion of patients, dosing could be reduced to once a day after 1 full year of twice-daily therapy without loss of benefit.

recommended_regimens.name: lifitegrast 5%
recommended_regimens.summary: Consider topical treatment for the signs and symptoms of dry eye.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: Published studies reported improvement in signs and/or symptoms over 3 months. The medicine appeared safe over 12 months, although longer-term effects were unknown.

recommended_regimens.name: Topical corticosteroid
recommended_regimens.summary: Low-dose topical treatment may be used intermittently for a short period to suppress ocular surface inflammation; monitor for increased intraocular pressure and cataract formation.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: Corticosteroids have been reported to reduce irritation and corneal fluorescein staining and to improve filamentary keratitis.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Infrequent intervals for short periods, such as several weeks

recommended_regimens.name: loteprednol etabonate 0.25%
recommended_regimens.summary: A prospective randomized study evaluated this topical corticosteroid for dry eye.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: The study found improvement in symptoms and conjunctival hyperemia over 2 weeks, but not in ocular surface staining, Schirmer test results, or artificial tear use. Treatment extended to 4 weeks produced no further benefit or increase in the side-effect profile.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: 2 weeks; extending treatment to 4 weeks showed no additional benefit

recommended_regimens.name: varenicline nasal spray
recommended_regimens.summary: An approved option for treating dry eye signs and symptoms through stimulation of tear production.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: A randomized phase-3 trial reported good tolerability and a clinically meaningful effect on dry eye signs and symptoms.

recommended_regimens.name: perfluorohexyloctane ophthalmic drops
recommended_regimens.summary: An approved, preservative-free option for dry eye signs and symptoms, including dry eye secondary to meibomian gland dysfunction.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: A randomized, multicenter, double-masked phase-3 trial found statistically significant improvements versus hypotonic saline in dry eye secondary to meibomian gland dysfunction. In another randomized study of 312 Chinese patients, drops given four times daily for 2 months significantly improved signs and symptoms versus 0.6% NaCl drops.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: In the study of 312 Chinese patients: four times daily for 2 months

recommended_regimens.name: Topical secretagogues
recommended_regimens.summary: Consider among prescription treatments when earlier options are inadequate.

alternative_regimens.name: Slow-release hydroxypropyl cellulose inserts
alternative_regimens.summary: Occasionally provide a helpful alternative to instilled tears.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Consider when the patient cannot apply artificial tears.

response_assessment.timepoint: At follow-up intervals determined by severity, treatment, and response
response_assessment.method: Assess symptoms, visual function, tear film and ocular surface findings, and treatment adverse effects.
response_assessment.interpretation: Modify treatment according to benefit, tolerability, and evidence of ocular surface damage.

supportive_care: Continue patient education and management of contributing causes.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The highlighted findings list lifitegrast 0.5%, whereas the detailed treatment discussion describes and reports approval of lifitegrast 5%. The guide states that approved treatments have not been proven superior to one another in direct prospective comparisons.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with dry eye and contributing meibomian gland dysfunction or meibomitis whose initial measures are inadequate.
decision_rules: Treat the contributing gland disease alongside tear-directed therapy.
If meibomian gland dysfunction is present, consider a lipid-containing lubricant.

recommended_regimens.name: Lipid-containing ocular lubricants
recommended_regimens.summary: Consider lipid-containing supplementation when meibomian gland dysfunction accompanies dry eye.

recommended_regimens.name: In-office heating and expression of the meibomian glands
recommended_regimens.summary: Consider physical gland heating and expression, including thermal pulsation devices, after initial measures prove inadequate.

recommended_regimens.name: Oral macrolide or tetracycline antibiotics
recommended_regimens.summary: Consider as prescription options in the staged management approach.

alternative_regimens.name: perfluorohexyloctane ophthalmic drops
alternative_regimens.summary: May treat signs and symptoms of dry eye secondary to meibomian gland dysfunction.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Consider for patients whose dry eye is associated with meibomian gland dysfunction.

supportive_care: Continue eyelid hygiene and warm compresses.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with dry eye in whom Demodex is present and initial measures are inadequate.
decision_rules: Use Demodex-directed treatment only when Demodex is present.

recommended_regimens.name: Tea tree oil
recommended_regimens.summary: Consider treatment directed at Demodex as part of the next management step.

recommended_regimens.name: lotilaner drops
recommended_regimens.summary: Consider drops directed at Demodex.

alternative_regimens.name: ivermectin 1% cream
alternative_regimens.summary: Listed as an off-label option directed at Demodex.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Demodex is present; use is off-label.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with dry eye and concurrent anterior blepharitis.
decision_rules: Treat contributing blepharitis rather than using tear replacement as the sole intervention.

recommended_regimens.name: Topical antibiotic or corticosteroid applied to the lid margins
recommended_regimens.summary: Consider treatment of the lid margins when anterior blepharitis is present.

supportive_care: Continue appropriate eyelid hygiene and warm compresses.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Associated eyelid abnormalities caused by blepharitis, trichiasis, or malposition should also be addressed.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with aqueous tear deficiency for whom medical measures to increase tear availability are ineffective or impractical.
decision_rules: Consider punctal occlusion after medical tear-enhancing approaches fail or cannot reasonably be used.
Punctal plugs are best placed after tear homeostasis has been achieved.
If a beneficial plug is spontaneously lost, consider replacement or permanent punctal closure.

recommended_regimens.name: Punctal occlusion
recommended_regimens.summary: Consider tear conservation with punctal plugs made of silicone, collagen, or thermal labile polymer. For silicone plugs, use the largest size that can be inserted to reduce extrusion.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: A Cochrane Collaboration review found limited evidence from seven randomized controlled trials that silicone plugs may relieve symptoms in severe dry eye. One study found that 56% of silicone plugs remained in place after 2 years; among patients whose plugs were spontaneously lost, 34% were reported to have canalicular stenosis at 2 years.

alternative_regimens.name: Moisture chamber spectacles/goggles
alternative_regimens.summary: Provide a noninvasive means of reducing tear loss.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Consider when tear conservation is needed.

alternative_regimens.name: Thermal labile polymer plugs
alternative_regimens.summary: Intracanalicular placement avoids direct irritation of the ocular surface, but epiphora, canaliculitis, dacryocystitis, and keratitis have been associated with these plugs.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Consider as a punctal-occlusion material while weighing its reported complications.

response_assessment.method: Assess symptom relief, ocular surface findings, plug retention, irritation, and epiphora.
response_assessment.interpretation: Silicone plugs can be removed if irritation or epiphora develops; a beneficial plug that is lost can be replaced or followed by permanent closure.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Whether plugs should be used when inflammatory ocular conditions such as rosacea conjunctivitis or allergic conjunctivitis coexist remains debated. A displaced plug can obstruct the lacrimal system and cause secondary infection, although surgical removal is rarely needed.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients for whom preceding management options remain inadequate, including patients with severe dry eye.
decision_rules: Continue useful earlier treatments and consider additional tear-derived products, therapeutic contact lenses, or oral secretagogues according to the patient's presentation.
Weigh contact lens handling, fitting difficulties, tolerability, and infection risk when selecting a therapeutic lens.

recommended_regimens.name: Oral secretagogues
recommended_regimens.summary: Consider systemic stimulation of secretion after preceding management options are inadequate.

recommended_regimens.name: Autologous/allogeneic serum eye drops
recommended_regimens.summary: Consider serum-based eye drops for disease that remains inadequately controlled.

recommended_regimens.name: Platelet-rich plasma eye drops
recommended_regimens.summary: Consider among blood-derived topical treatments at this management step.

recommended_regimens.name: Blood based products
recommended_regimens.summary: Consider other blood-derived products when earlier measures do not adequately control disease.

recommended_regimens.name: Rigid scleral lenses
recommended_regimens.summary: Consider therapeutic scleral lenses for severe dry eye.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: The guide reports successful use in severe dry eye.

alternative_regimens.name: Soft bandage lenses
alternative_regimens.summary: May provide symptomatic relief in selected patients, but require caution because of infection risk, particularly with extended wear.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Consider when a therapeutic contact lens is suitable and its risks are acceptable.

alternative_regimens.name: Allogeneic serum eye drops
alternative_regimens.summary: Reported as an effective and safe alternative to autologous serum.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Consider when repeated blood sampling is not possible.

response_assessment.timepoint: At follow-up intervals determined by severity, treatment, and response
response_assessment.method: Assess symptom control, visual function, ocular surface damage, lens tolerance where applicable, and the need to change treatment.
response_assessment.interpretation: More severe disease or complications can require closer follow-up.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Scleral lens use may be limited by fitting difficulties, particularly with conjunctival cicatrization, as well as cost and the patient's ability or willingness to insert and remove the lenses.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with severe dry eye for whom earlier management steps are inadequate.
decision_rules: Consider longer-duration topical corticosteroid treatment, amniotic membrane grafting, permanent punctal occlusion, or other surgery when preceding options do not adequately control disease.
Before planned cautery, generally perform temporary occlusion to assess whether epiphora develops.
For cautery, a staged approach is generally recommended.

recommended_regimens.name: Topical corticosteroid
recommended_regimens.summary: Consider a longer course for severe disease unresponsive to preceding options.

recommended_regimens.name: Amniotic membrane grafts
recommended_regimens.summary: Consider for severe disease inadequately controlled with preceding approaches.

recommended_regimens.name: Surgical punctal occlusion (punctal cautery)
recommended_regimens.summary: Consider permanent closure. Thermal cautery is generally more effective than laser cautery for complete permanent occlusion; cautery is not readily reversible.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: No more than one punctum in each eye at a treatment session

recommended_regimens.name: tarsorrhaphy
recommended_regimens.summary: A limited procedure may reduce tear film instability when other therapies have failed.

recommended_regimens.name: minor salivary gland transplantation
recommended_regimens.summary: Consider among other surgical approaches for disease inadequately controlled with preceding treatment.

alternative_regimens.name: Laser cautery
alternative_regimens.summary: Can produce permanent punctal occlusion, but is generally less effective and more expensive than thermal cautery.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: An alternative means of cautery when permanent occlusion is planned.

response_assessment.method: Generally use nonpermanent implants, particularly silicone plugs, as a trial of occlusion.
response_assessment.interpretation: Assess for the development of epiphora.

response_assessment.method: Evaluate symptoms, vision, ocular surface damage, and adverse effects.
response_assessment.interpretation: Adjust treatment and follow-up frequency according to severity and response.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Patients with sterile corneal ulceration associated with dry eye may require daily follow-up.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with severe dry eye associated with Sjögren’s syndrome, particularly those who also have dry mouth.
decision_rules: Choose ocular treatment according to the relative contributions of deficient aqueous production and evaporative loss, ocular surface damage, and disease severity.
Arrange management of the systemic disease with a rheumatologist.
Set expectations that oral secretagogues generally improve dry mouth more than dry eye.

recommended_regimens.name: Autologous serum and autologous plasma rich in growth factors drops
recommended_regimens.summary: Reported to improve ocular irritation and conjunctival and corneal staining in patients with Sjögren’s syndrome.

recommended_regimens.name: Oral secretagogues
recommended_regimens.summary: Available for severe dryness, especially when ocular and oral dryness coexist.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: Clinical studies generally found greater improvement in oral than ocular dryness.

recommended_regimens.name: cevimeline
recommended_regimens.summary: Approved for dry-mouth symptoms in Sjögren’s syndrome; it has also been found to improve ocular irritation and aqueous tear production and may cause fewer systemic adverse effects than oral pilocarpine.

recommended_regimens.name: pilocarpine
recommended_regimens.summary: Oral treatment was evaluated for visual symptoms in patients with Sjogren syndrome.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: At 5 mg orally four times a day, treated patients had significantly greater overall improvement than placebo recipients in focusing while reading and blurred vision, but no improvement in light sensitivity, ocular discomfort, or other dry eye symptoms. Excessive sweating occurred in over 40% of patients; Two percent withdrew because of this or other treatment-related adverse effects.

alternative_regimens.name: Autologous serum 20%
alternative_regimens.summary: A systematic review reported a symptom benefit compared with artificial tears.

alternative_regimens.name: Topical lubricants, topical anti-inflammatory therapy, and tear-conserving strategies
alternative_regimens.summary: An outcomes-based review described these approaches as apparently effective despite a shortage of rigorous clinical trials.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Select according to dry eye characteristics and severity.

not_recommended.name: Anti-tumor necrosis factor agents
not_recommended.reason: A systematic review did not find them effective for the sicca features discussed.

response_assessment.method: Assess discomfort, visual disturbance, tear production and evaporation, tear film stability, lid margin disease, and ocular surface damage.
response_assessment.interpretation: Use the findings to guide treatment selection and adjustment.

supportive_care: Educate the patient about aggravating factors and realistic treatment goals.
Coordinate care with a rheumatologist for associated systemic disease.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guide reports no strong evidence that oral hydroxychloroquine treats dry eye in Sjögren’s syndrome, although it is commonly prescribed for fatigue and arthralgias. It also describes evidence for rituximab efficacy as not strong.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with severe dry eye associated with GVHD.
decision_rules: Consider blood-derived topical treatment when severe dry eye warrants escalation.

recommended_regimens.name: Autologous serum and autologous plasma rich in growth factors drops
recommended_regimens.summary: Reported to improve ocular irritation and conjunctival and corneal dye staining in patients with GVHD.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with filamentary keratitis accompanying severe dry eye.
decision_rules: Remove filaments and consider treatment of viscous mucus.
Consider a protective contact lens to prevent recurrence, while accounting for tolerance and infection risk.
In refractory cases, consider amniotic membrane placement while recognizing that its effect is short-term.

recommended_regimens.name: Filament debridement
recommended_regimens.summary: Remove filaments using a moistened cotton-tip applicator, dry cellulose sponge, or forceps.

recommended_regimens.name: N-acetylcysteine 10%
recommended_regimens.summary: A topical mucolytic may reduce the viscosity of the mucinous tear film.

recommended_regimens.name: Soft contact lenses
recommended_regimens.summary: Can prevent recurrence of filamentary keratitis, although patients with severe dry eye may tolerate them poorly.

alternative_regimens.name: Self-retaining or sutureless amniotic membrane
alternative_regimens.summary: May be considered, with the understanding that its effect is short-term.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Use contact lenses cautiously if neurotrophic keratopathy is also present because of infection risk.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with suspected neuropathic ocular pain and a peripheral pain component.
decision_rules: First assess the ocular surface and tear parameters for nociceptive sources of pain.
If pain is present before an anesthetic drop and improves afterward, a nociceptive or peripheral neuropathic component is suggested.
Select treatment according to the suspected location of nerve dysfunction.

recommended_regimens.name: Autologous serum tears
recommended_regimens.summary: A topical nerve-regenerative option for peripheral neuropathic ocular pain.

response_assessment.method: Examine tear parameters and the ocular surface, compare symptoms with observed signs, and consider an anesthetic challenge when pain is present.
response_assessment.interpretation: Improvement after anesthetic suggests a nociceptive or peripheral neuropathic contribution; lack of improvement suggests a central or nonocular cause.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Neuropathic pain can coexist with tear deficiency or meibomian gland dysfunction; symptoms may be disproportionate to visible ocular findings.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with a central pain component or systemic comorbidities such as fibromyalgia; specific adjunctive options are described for light sensitivity with headache or for cutaneous allodynia or postsurgical pain.
decision_rules: Consider oral neuromodulators when pain has a central component or systemic comorbidities.
Consider migraine-directed adjuncts for light sensitivity and headache, and periocular nerve blocks for cutaneous allodynia or postsurgical pain.
A combination of approaches is often used; explain that neuromodulators do not provide immediate relief.

recommended_regimens.name: pregabalin, gabapentin, duloxetine, amitriptyline, nortriptyline, low-dose naltrexone
recommended_regimens.summary: These oral neuromodulators have been used individually or together, with varying success.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: About 3 to 4 months at a therapeutic dose may be needed to observe pain reduction.

alternative_regimens.name: Transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation device
alternative_regimens.summary: May be considered as an adjunctive migraine-directed strategy.

alternative_regimens.name: Periorbital botulinum toxin A injections
alternative_regimens.summary: May be considered as an adjunctive migraine-directed strategy.

alternative_regimens.name: Periocular nerve blocks consisting of a corticosteroid with a long-acting sodium channel blocker
alternative_regimens.summary: May be used for a localized pain presentation.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Cutaneous allodynia around the eye or postsurgical pain.

alternative_regimens.name: Acupuncture, cognitive behavioral therapy, or hypnosis
alternative_regimens.summary: Consider complementary approaches when emotional or mood-related difficulties accompany chronic pain.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Concomitant anxiety, depression, or other mood disorders.

response_assessment.timepoint: About 3 to 4 months at a therapeutic dose
response_assessment.method: Assess change in pain after an adequate course of oral neuromodulation.
response_assessment.interpretation: An immediate lack of relief does not establish that a neuromodulator has failed.

supportive_care: Set expectations early about the time needed for neuromodulators to work.
Use a multidisciplinary approach involving relevant eye care, pain, neurology, and mental health professionals.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients considering keratorefractive surgery, particularly LASIK, or lens-based surgery.
decision_rules: Evaluate and manage dry eye before and after lens-based surgery.
Treat dry eye effectively before keratorefractive surgery and explain that surgery may worsen symptoms.
Do not proceed with keratorefractive surgery while dry eye syndrome is uncontrolled.

recommended_regimens.name: Preoperative dry eye assessment and treatment
recommended_regimens.summary: Identify and improve contributing factors before surgery when possible; continue postoperative evaluation and management for lens-based surgery.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: Dry eye symptoms persisting beyond the normal postoperative period of 3 months occur in about one third of individuals following intraocular refractive and/or cataract surgery.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Before surgery and, for lens-based surgery, after surgery

not_recommended.name: Keratorefractive surgery in patients with uncontrolled dry eye syndrome
not_recommended.reason: Uncontrolled dry eye syndrome is a contraindication; keratorefractive surgery may worsen existing symptoms.

response_assessment.method: Assess dry eye symptoms, tear film, and the ocular surface.
response_assessment.interpretation: Baseline ocular surface and tear film parameters help identify patients at risk of postoperative dry eye.

supportive_care: Counsel patients that symptoms are common during the first few months after keratorefractive or lens-based surgery and often lessen with time.

artifacts.title: TABLE 1 CHARACTERISTIC FINDINGS FOR DRY EYE SYNDROME DIAGNOSTIC TESTS

rows: Aqueous tear production (Schirmer test)

Schirmer I test (without anesthesia), measures both basic and reflex tearing. Less than 5.5 mm of wetting after 5 minutes is diagnostic of aqueous tear deficiency. Schirmer II test (with anesthesia) measures reflex secretion by stimulating nasal mucosa with cotton-tip applicator. Wetting of less than 15 mm after 2 minutes is considered abnormal. (See Appendix 5 for additional information.)
Fluorescein dye disappearance test/tear function index
Test result is compared with a standard color scale.
Fluorescein tear break-up time
Less than 10 seconds is considered abnormal.
Ocular surface dye staining (example: fluorescein, lissamine, rose bengal)
Staining of inferior cornea and bulbar conjunctiva within the palpebral fissure is typical.
Lacrimal gland function
Indicates decreased tear lactoferrin concentration.
Tear osmolarity
Elevated; test-to-test variability; differences between the eyes are considered abnormal.
Matrix metalloproteinase-9
Indicates presence of inflammation.

artifacts.description: The findings listed for each test address tear production, clearance, film stability, ocular surface staining, lacrimal gland function, osmolarity, or inflammation. The guideline cautions against establishing dry eye syndrome from any single test alone.

recommendations.statement: Evaluate and manage dry eye before and after lens-based surgery.
recommendations.context: Applies to all patients undergoing lens-based surgery.
recommendations.rationale: Preoperative ocular surface and tear film findings help identify patients at risk of postoperative symptoms.
recommendations.source_heading: HIGHLIGHTED FINDINGS AND RECOMMENDATIONS FOR CARE

recommendations.statement: Inform patients with dry eye syndrome who are considering keratorefractive or lens-based surgery that their symptoms may worsen afterward.
recommendations.rationale: Dry eye symptoms are common during the first few postoperative months, although they often lessen over time.
recommendations.source_heading: HIGHLIGHTED FINDINGS AND RECOMMENDATIONS FOR CARE

recommendations.statement: Address pre-existing contributors to dry eye syndrome before keratorefractive or lens-based surgery when they can be improved.
recommendations.rationale: Preoperative improvement of contributing factors can reduce the likelihood of worsening dry eye.
recommendations.source_heading: HIGHLIGHTED FINDINGS AND RECOMMENDATIONS FOR CARE

recommendations.statement: Consider congenital, autoimmune, dermatologic, endocrine, nutritional, medication-related, post-infectious, and environmental contributors when assessing pediatric dry eye.
recommendations.context: Pediatric patients with suspected dry eye disease.
recommendations.rationale: Dry eye disease can be overlooked in children.

recommendations.statement: Maintain strong suspicion for Sjӧgren’s syndrome in patients with clinically significant dry eye, and use a low threshold for diagnostic serological evaluation.
recommendations.rationale: Underlying Sjӧgren’s syndrome is associated with an increased risk of lymphoid malignancy.

recommendations.statement: Provide a comprehensive medical eye evaluation and follow-up at recommended intervals, including assessment of the tear film and ocular surface.
recommendations.context: Tear film and ocular surface assessment is particularly important before cataract or refractive surgery.

recommendations.statement: Perform additional testing relevant to dry eye when a patient presents with suggestive symptoms.
Perform a detailed review of systems for patients with clinically significant dry eye, and select diagnostic tests according to that review and the clinical findings.
Assess corneal sensation when trigeminal nerve dysfunction is suspected.
Interpret tear osmolarity alongside clinical findings or changes across time or conditions rather than relying on one measurement to confirm dry eye.
recommendations.rationale: Osmolarity may vary and may not consistently correspond to symptoms or clinical signs.

recommendations.statement: Consider laboratory and clinical evaluation for autoimmune disorders when significant dry eye occurs with other autoimmune features, such as dry mouth, or with a family history of autoimmune disease.
Order serological testing for SSA or anti-Ro, SSB or anti-La, rheumatoid factor, and antinuclear antibody when Sjӧgren’s syndrome is suspected.
recommendations.context: Maintain particular suspicion when clinically significant dry eye occurs with dry mouth.

recommendations.statement: Test for antithyroid peroxidase antibody and antithyroglobulin antibody when thyroid eye disease is suspected.
Use orbital CT or MRI scans when needed to assess extraocular muscle thickening in patients with thyroid disease.
Perform a conjunctival biopsy in patients with significant chronic conjunctivitis accompanied by nodularity or cicatrization.
recommendations.context: Cicatrization includes subepithelial fibrosis or fornix foreshortening.

recommendations.statement: Treat identifiable contributors to dry eye when they are amenable to treatment rather than relying on tear replacement alone.
recommendations.rationale: Tear replacement alone is often unsuccessful if additional causes remain unaddressed.

recommendations.statement: Explain the natural history and chronic course of dry eye to patients, and discuss realistic treatment goals with them.
recommendations.rationale: Patient education is important to successful management.

recommendations.statement: At Step 1, consider education about the condition, treatment, management, and prognosis; changes to the local environment; discussion of dietary changes, including oral essential fatty acid supplementation; review and potential modification or removal of contributing systemic or topical medications; ocular lubricants, including lipid-containing supplements when MGD is present; and eyelid hygiene with warm compresses.
recommendations.context: The staged options are not exclusive. Severity, etiology, clinician experience, and patient preference guide selection; options can be chosen across steps or combined within a step.

recommendations.statement: If Step 1 measures are inadequate, consider nonpreserved ocular lubricants; treatment of Demodex, when present, with tea tree oil or lotilaner drops or off-label ivermectin 1% cream; punctal occlusion or moisture chamber eyewear; overnight ointment or moisture chamber devices; and in-office heating and expression of the meibomian glands, including thermal pulsation devices.
recommendations.context: Step 2 options may be combined or selected from different steps according to disease severity and etiology.
recommendations.rationale: Nonpreserved lubricants can limit preservative-induced toxicity.
