document_sections.heading: ## METHODS AND KEY TO RATINGS
document_sections.content: The guideline uses methods from SIGN to grade individual studies and GRADE to assess the evidence supporting care recommendations. Individual-study ratings are I++ for high-quality meta-analyses, systematic reviews of randomized controlled trials, or trials with very low bias risk; I+ for well-conducted versions with low bias risk; I- for versions with high bias risk; II++ for high-quality reviews or studies of case-control or cohort designs with very low confounding or bias risk and a high probability of causality; II+ for well-conducted case-control or cohort studies with low confounding or bias risk and a moderate probability of causality; II- for such studies with high confounding or bias risk and substantial risk that the relationship is not causal; and III for nonanalytic studies. GRADE labels the overall evidence Good quality when further research is very unlikely to change confidence in the effect estimate, Moderate quality when further research is likely to affect confidence substantially and may change the estimate, and Insufficient quality when further research is very likely to affect confidence substantially, probably change the estimate, and any estimate is highly uncertain. A Strong recommendation applies when desirable effects clearly outweigh undesirable effects, or clearly do not; a Discretionary recommendation applies when trade-offs are less certain because evidence quality is low or effects are closely balanced. Ratings appear throughout the main text. PubMed update searches took place on March 3, 2022 and June 7, 2023. Recommendations draw on systematic reviews and consideration of benefits, harms, and their balance; final decisions use informal consensus, with voting when disagreement remains and abstention by members with direct financial relationships in the disputed area.

document_sections.heading: ## HIGHLIGHTED FINDINGS AND RECOMMENDATIONS FOR CARE
document_sections.content: Dry eye syndrome commonly causes discomfort and visual impairment that substantially diminish quality of life; it can also compromise cataract, corneal, and keratorefractive surgical results. Clinical examination remains the diagnostic gold standard: no individual test establishes dry eye, whereas combined findings can clarify the condition. Drug and procedural therapies can improve symptoms and signs, but cure is uncommon and prolonged treatment is usually needed. FDA-approved options identified here are topical loteprednol 0.25%, lifitegrast 0.5%, cyclosporine 0.05% and 0.09%, varenicline nasal spray, and perflurohexyloctane ophthalmic solution. They may improve symptoms and/or signs; none has been shown superior to another in head-to-head trials, and the literature lacks a direct prospective clinical-trial comparison. Patients contemplating keratorefractive or lens-based surgery should be warned that symptoms may worsen afterward. Improving contributory factors before surgery may reduce that risk. Symptoms are common during the first few postoperative months and often diminish. Dry eye is a major contributor to dissatisfaction after intraocular refractive and/or cataract surgery; symptoms persist beyond the usual postoperative period of 3 months in about one third of individuals. Baseline ocular-surface and tear-film measures predict risk, so every lens-based surgery patient should undergo dry-eye assessment and management both before and after surgery. Approximately 10% of patients with clinically aqueous tear deficiency dry eye have underlying Sjӧgren’s syndrome. A cited meta-analysis found primary Sjӧgren’s syndrome to have the strongest association with lymphoid proliferative malignancy among autoimmune diseases.

document_sections.heading: DISEASE DEFINITION
document_sections.content: Dry eye syndrome, also called dry eye disease or keratoconjunctivitis sicca, encompasses tear-film disorders arising from reduced production and/or instability of tears, accompanied by ocular discomfort and/or visual symptoms and inflammatory disease of the ocular surface.

document_sections.heading: PATIENT POPULATION
document_sections.content: The population includes people of any age with findings suggestive of dry eye, including burning, gritty or sandy irritation, redness, mucus discharge, variable vision, a reduced tear meniscus, or meibomian gland stasis and/or obstruction. Similar symptoms do not establish that a patient has dry eye.

document_sections.heading: CLINICAL OBJECTIVES
document_sections.content: Clinical aims are to diagnose dry eye while distinguishing other causes of irritation and redness; identify local, systemic, environmental, and lifestyle contributors; select appropriate therapy; relieve discomfort; prevent deterioration in vision, symptoms, and examination findings; and educate and involve patients in managing their condition.

document_sections.heading: PREVALENCE AND RISK FACTORS
document_sections.content: Prevalence estimates are constrained by inconsistent disease definitions and the absence of a definitive single test or test combination. In one clinic series, 17% of 2,127 consecutive new patients received a diagnosis after comprehensive examination, although clinic findings may not represent the general population. An Australian population study of 926 people aged 40 to 97 years found a low Schirmer result (≤8 mm) in 16.3% and a high rose bengal result (≥4 van Bijsterveld score) in 10.8%. Among 3,722 Beaver Dam Eye Study participants, self-reported prevalence ranged from 8.4% below age 60 years to 19.0% above age 80 years, with 14.4% overall. In the Men’s Health Study (n = 25,444), prevalence rose from 3.9% at ages 50 to 54 years to 7.7% above age 80; its definition required a reported clinical diagnosis or frequent or constant dryness together with irritation. Using the same definition, a Women’s Health Study of over 39,000 women found 5.7% below age 50 and 9.8% above age 75. Among 224 clinic patients identified with dry eye, signs of meibomian-gland-related evaporative disease were much more likely than signs of isolated aqueous deficiency. Claims covering nearly 10 million managed-care enrollees identified diagnosis or punctal-occlusion treatment in 0.4% to 0.5%. Older age and female gender are major risk factors. Cited studies associate dry eye with visual display terminal use among Japanese office workers, glaucoma medication containing benzalkonium chloride, rheumatoid arthritis, and sleep disorders; sedative-hypnotic use might contribute. After age and gender adjustment, the Beaver Dam Eye Study associated smoking and multivitamin use with higher risk and caffeine use with lower risk. Its update additionally associated antihistamines, antidepressant and antianxiety medications, and oral corticosteroids with dry eye, while angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors were associated with lower risk. Among 25,665 postmenopausal Women’s Health Study participants, hormone replacement therapy, particularly estrogen alone, was associated with greater risk of a clinical diagnosis or severe symptoms (I+, Moderate, Discretionary). A Chinese community study found 17.5% prevalence among patients with diabetes, whose mean age was 68.9 ± 8.9 years, especially with poor metabolic control. Pediatric dry eye may be missed because prevalence is low, awareness is limited, and examination cooperation can be difficult. Its possible associations include congenital, autoimmune, dermatologic, endocrine, nutritional, medication-related, and post-infectious causes, including alacrima, ectodermal dysplasia, familial dysautonomia, juvenile rheumatoid arthritis, Sjögren's syndrome, acne rosacea, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, vitamin A deficiency, malabsorption, restricted diets, oral isotretinoin therapy for acne vulgaris, measles, and EpsteinBarr virus. Allergy and prolonged screen use may cause or aggravate pediatric dry eye.

document_sections.heading: PATHOGENESIS
document_sections.content: The ocular surface and tear-secreting glands operate together as a lacrimal functional unit. Dysfunction can destabilize the tear film, produce irritation, and damage surface epithelium. Potential contributors include aging, diminished androgen support, blink or eyelid abnormalities, systemic inflammation such as Sjӧgren’s syndrome, autoimmune thyroid disease or rheumatoid arthritis, ocular disease such as HSV keratitis, procedures disrupting trigeminal sensory input such as LASIK or SMILE, and diseases or drugs disrupting cholinergic stimulation of secretion. Reduced tear production and clearance initiate ocular-surface inflammation involving cellular and soluble mediators; clinical and basic research suggests inflammation contributes to disease. Zhang et al proposed in 2017 that tissues, cells, matrices, and the microbiome form an ocular-surface microenvironment whose disturbed homeostasis can produce dry eye; under that hypothesis, therapy should restore its homeostasis. The 2017 DEWS II report identified deficient aqueous production and tear-film instability as independently sufficient factors that may also coexist. Tear-film instability appears more common, but aqueous deficiency remains important because it may accompany systemic inflammatory or autoimmune illness. Most patients have multiple contributors; neurotrophic keratitis after HSV or VZV infection or LASIK can involve both diminished production and greater evaporation.

document_sections.heading: ASSOCIATED CONDITIONS
document_sections.content: Diuretics, antihistamines, anticholinergics, antidepressants, and systemic retinoids such as isotretinoin may aggravate symptoms. Frequently instilled eye medicines, for example more than four drops a day, can disturb tear-film maintenance, with preservatives contributing to epithelial breakdown. Low humidity, wind, drafts, air conditioning, heating, and reduced blinking during prolonged screen use, reading, or driving may worsen discomfort. External irritants and allergens may aggravate symptoms without being considered causes. Rosacea can worsen dry eye and ocular-surface disease. Although more frequently observed in fair skin, it occurs in all skin types; findings include facial erythema, telangiectasia, papules, pustules, enlarged sebaceous glands, and rhinophyma. Darker skin may obscure flushing and telangiectasia. Children may develop ocular manifestations before obvious skin disease, allowing misdiagnosis. Rosacea is more prevalent in women but can be more severe in men. Subtle signs can be overlooked, particularly in children presenting with recurrent blepharokeratoconjunctivitis, punctate erosions, peripheral keratitis, meibomian gland disease, or recurrent chalazia. Pediatric ocular disease often includes asymmetric corneal involvement with potentially sight-threatening impairment; skin manifestations are less frequent and atopy is common. Childhood styes are associated with increased adult rosacea risk. In Sjögren's syndrome, inflammatory infiltration of exocrine glands impairs salivary and tear production. About 10% of patients with clinically significant aqueous deficient dry eye have underlying primary Sjӧgren’s syndrome. Primary disease is multisystemic and increases lymphoma risk; about 5% of patients with Sjögren syndrome develop a lymphoid malignancy. A cited meta-analysis found the strongest rheumatic-disease association with lymphoid malignancy for primary Sjӧgren’s syndrome, reporting an incidence rate of 18.9% (95% CI, 9.4–37.9) and an increased incidence of 320 cases per 100,000 patient years. Ophthalmologists should therefore maintain strong suspicion and a low threshold for diagnostic serology in clinically significant dry eye. Infiltration or replacement of lacrimal secretory tissue in lymphoma, sarcoidosis, hemochromatosis, or amyloidosis can cause aqueous deficiency. Dry eye has also been reported with Epstein-Barr virus, human T-cell lymphotropic virus type 1, HIV, hepatitis C, and hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, with or without GVHD. One AIDS group had dry eye in 21%; diffuse infiltrative lymphadenopathy syndrome has been described in HIV, predominantly among children. Hepatitis C has been associated with decreased secretion and tear lactoferrin. Primary or persistent Epstein-Barr virus infection has been linked to gland enlargement, dry eye, and Sjögren’s syndrome. Chronic GVHD can cause lacrimal and conjunctival infiltration and fibrosis through T-cell interaction with fibroblasts. Ocular mucous membrane pemphigoid and Stevens-Johnson syndrome may destroy conjunctival goblet cells through inflammation and scarring. Atopy may contribute through blepharitis, conjunctival scarring, or antihistamines. Dry eye in younger patients or males warrants suspicion of an associated local or systemic disorder. Relevant eyelid or neurologic conditions include malposition, lagophthalmos, exophthalmos, thyroid-associated ocular disease, blepharitis, Parkinson disease, and Bell’s palsy; orbital or eyelid surgery, radiation, and injury may also contribute. Incomplete blinking was associated with a two-fold increase in evaporative dry eye, greater meibomian gland loss, poorer meibum, and thinner tear-film lipid layer. Greater screen exposure can reduce blinking and worsen ocular-surface disease in adults and children.

document_sections.heading: NATURAL HISTORY
document_sections.content: Severity, duration, and cause vary. For the majority, dry eye does not threaten sight, although vision fluctuates and irritation commonly intensifies toward day's end. Drugs that suppress tear secretion or environments that destabilize the tear film can cause abrupt worsening; removing these factors often produces marked improvement. Symptoms can fluctuate chronically or gradually intensify. Clinically significant disease may produce reversible conjunctival squamous metaplasia and punctate conjunctival or corneal erosions detectable by dye staining. Severe disease accompanying systemic inflammation may lead to keratinization, conjunctival fibrosis or cicatrization, limbal stem cell deficiency, corneal scarring, thinning, neovascularization, microbial or sterile ulceration with possible perforation, and severe visual loss.

document_sections.heading: PATIENT OUTCOME CRITERIA
document_sections.content: Treatment outcomes include reducing irritation, redness, mucus discharge, and other dry-eye findings; preserving or improving visual function; and limiting or preventing ocular-surface injury.

document_sections.heading: DIAGNOSIS
document_sections.content: Other ocular-surface diseases can mimic dry eye through foreign-body sensation, mild itching, irritation, or soreness. Environments such as air travel, low humidity, drafts, or poorly fitted sleep apnea devices; prolonged reading or digital-device use; and relief with artificial tears can inform diagnosis. Examination findings and tests support confirmation. The classification diagram distinguishes dry eye disease from other ocular-surface disease.

document_sections.heading: History
document_sections.content: Relevant symptoms include irritation, tearing, burning, stinging, dryness or foreign-body sensation, mild itching, photophobia, blurred vision, contact lens intolerance, redness, mucus, increased blinking, fatigue, and variation during the day, especially later worsening. History should address duration and aggravation by air travel, low humidity, fans, prolonged visual concentration with reduced blinking, digital devices, or ill-fitting sleep apnea devices. NEI-VFQ25 assesses vision-related quality of life, including periocular irritation. OSDI covers ocular symptoms, vision-related functioning, and environmental triggers; its reported specificity is 0.83 and sensitivity 0.60 for distinguishing dry eye from normal eyes. SPEED was designed to track symptoms over time and, when evaluated against OSDI symptom-based grouping, yielded sensitivity 0.90 and specificity 0.80. Ocular history may cover topical treatments and preservatives, contact lenses, allergic conjunctivitis, corneal or cataract or refractive procedures, HSV, VZV, ocular mucous membrane pemphigoid, aniridia, prior eyelid operations, Bell’s palsy, cranial nerve injury, and eye cosmetics. Medical and symptom review may cover screens, active or passive smoke, rosacea, psoriasis, varicella zoster virus, face and eyelid cleansing, atopy, systemic inflammatory or other disease, systemic drugs including dupilumab and anticholinergic agents, trauma, chronic hepatitis C or HIV, transplantation and other nonocular surgery, orbital radiation, neurologic disease, nutrition including vitamin A deficiency and severely limited diets, gastrointestinal surgery, dry mouth, dental cavities, oral ulcers, fatigue, musculoskeletal symptoms, and menopause.

document_sections.heading: Examination
document_sections.content: Every patient should receive comprehensive medical eye assessment and follow-up at recommended intervals, including tear-film and ocular-surface evaluation, particularly before cataract or refractive surgery. Symptoms suggestive of dry eye warrant additional relevant tests. External and slit-lamp examinations document signs, tear quality, quantity, and stability, and alternative causes. External assessment may inspect skin for scleroderma, rosacea, or seborrhea; lids for closure, position, blinking, inflammation, secretions, or spasm; everted lids for tarsal conjunctival inflammation, allergy, or fibrosis; lacrimal-gland enlargement, proptosis, cranial nerves, and hand findings associated with systemic disease. Slit-lamp assessment addresses tear-meniscus height, debris, viscosity, mucus, foaming, and tear breakup; eyelash disorders; meibomian-gland openings, expressibility, atrophy, secretion, and lid-margin changes; punctal position, patency, or plugs; tarsal and bulbar conjunctival inflammation, scarring, staining, or other abnormalities; and corneal drying, dye staining, epithelial defects, filaments, thinning, infiltrates, ulcers, scarring, neovascularization, or prior surgery. Conjunctival lissamine green staining may assist early recognition of Sjögren’s syndrome.

document_sections.heading: Diagnostic Tests
document_sections.content: Clinically significant dry eye warrants detailed systems review, with tests selected according to associated findings. Table 1 relates each dry-eye diagnostic test to its characteristic findings. An assessment may use tear osmolarity, point-of-care matrix metalloproteinase-9, Schirmer testing with or without anesthesia, fluorescein disappearance, tear break-up time, surface dye staining, meibomian expressibility, or lacrimal-gland function. Schirmer I wetting of less than 5.5 mm after 5 minutes supports aqueous deficiency; Schirmer II wetting of less than 15 mm after 2 minutes is abnormal. Tear break-up time below 10 seconds is abnormal, although rapid breakup can coexist with normal aqueous production and little or no staining. Evaluate corneal sensation if trigeminal dysfunction is suspected. Osmolarity testing can identify instability, hyperosmolarity, or inter-eye differences, but its relationship to signs and symptoms varies. Findings over time, across conditions, and alongside clinical observations are more informative than a single result. Studies report stable osmolarity in normal eyes but rapidly varying results in dry eye with environmental change, consistent with evaporation-related hyperosmolarity as a mechanism of instability. Point-of-care matrix metalloproteinase-9 may assist diagnosis and assessment of disease change, but cannot distinguish dry eye from other inflammatory surface diseases. Consider laboratory and clinical evaluation for autoimmune disease when substantial dry eye accompanies suggestive symptoms, such as dry mouth, or autoimmune family history. Table 2 pairs suspected Sjögren’s syndrome, thyroid eye disease, sarcoidosis, and ocular mucous membrane pemphigoid with proposed testing. Clinically significant dry eye with dry mouth merits particular suspicion of Sjögren’s syndrome; suspected cases should receive SSA, SSB, rheumatoid factor, and antinuclear antibody serology. A point-of-care assay also includes SP1, CA6, and PSP, but further study is needed to establish whether these, particularly CA6, indicate early Sjögren’s syndrome or another autoimmune dry-eye form. Possible thyroid eye disease warrants antithyroid peroxidase antibody and antithyroglobulin antibody testing; CT or MRI may assess extraocular-muscle thickening in thyroid disease. Conjunctival biopsy is appropriate with significant chronic nodular or cicatrizing conjunctivitis. Noncontact instruments can image meibomian glands and assess tear breakup, meniscus, lipid layer, or blink completeness; white light interferometry can assess the tear film by reflected color.

document_sections.heading: CLASSIFICATION OF DRY EYE SYNDROME
document_sections.content: This guideline grades dry eye as mild, moderate, or severe using symptoms and signs, with greater emphasis on symptoms; overlapping features make the distinctions imprecise. Mild disease may cause intermittent irritation, itching, soreness, burning, discomfort, or blurred vision. Weak symptom–sign correlation complicates diagnosis, and patients may describe contact-lens-related dysesthesia or other conditions as dryness despite normal tear function. Distinguishing alternative causes improves the likelihood of symptom relief; repeated observation and symptom reports help establish a diagnosis over a usually chronic course. Moderate disease increases symptom frequency and discomfort and may affect visual functioning more consistently. Severe disease can bring frequent or constant, potentially disabling visual symptoms. Aqueous tear deficiency and evaporative dry eye are the two forms; both coexist in the majority of patients.

document_sections.heading: MANAGEMENT
document_sections.content: Multiple factors often contribute to symptoms, so treat modifiable causes alongside tear replacement; replacement alone frequently fails if other causes persist. Explain the chronic natural history and agree on realistic treatment aims with the patient. Table 3 presents staged management, but options from any step can be chosen at any severity according to clinical judgment and preference. Its Step 1 includes education, environmental and potential dietary changes, review of offending drugs, lubricants tailored to meibomian gland dysfunction when present, and lid hygiene with warm compresses. If insufficient, Step 2 includes nonpreserved lubricants, Demodex-directed treatment when indicated, tear conservation, overnight measures, meibomian-gland heating and expression, and indicated prescription treatments. Step 3 adds oral secretagogues, blood-based drops, and selected therapeutic lenses when previous options do not suffice. Step 4 adds longer topical corticosteroid use, amniotic membrane, surgical punctal closure, or other operations when earlier options remain inadequate. More than one option can be used concurrently; choices are not ranked within a category. Severity and cause determine selection, and evidence differs between therapies, especially newer ones. Prescription treatment should reflect the patient's presentation and indication-specific evidence.

document_sections.heading: Mild Dry Eye
document_sections.content: When symptoms suggest dry eye but signs are absent, trial artificial tears after excluding other sources of irritation, given imperfect tests and symptom–sign correlation. With clinically diagnosed mild disease, address potentially aggravating medicines, smoking or passive smoke, drafts, and low humidity. Smoking has been associated with changes affecting precorneal tear lipids and tear proteins. Humidifying air, shielding eyes, modifying airflow, lowering a computer display below eye level, taking regular breaks, consciously blinking fully, and using moisture-chamber goggles may help selected patients. As severity rises, topical aqueous enhancement with emulsions, gels, or ointments is appropriate; thicker preparations tend to last longer and require fewer applications but may blur vision more. Frequency of instillation must account for lifestyle and dexterity. Preserved substitutes may suffice for mild disease with an otherwise healthy surface; nonpreserved substitutes are generally recommended for chronic, frequent use, for example more than four times a day. A cited systematic review found artificial tears safe and effective, with most preparations appearing comparably effective, while cautioning about substantial inconsistency in study design and reporting. Treat contributory blepharitis or meibomitis and correct relevant trichiasis or lid malposition.

document_sections.heading: Moderate Dry Eye
document_sections.content: Options for moderate disease supplement mild-disease care; anti-inflammatory treatment may be considered alongside aqueous enhancement. Cyclosporine inhibits pathways involved in T-cell activation, inflammatory cytokine production, and mitochondrial apoptosis. One cited study found topical cyclosporine 0.05% produced a statistically significant 10-mm Schirmer increase versus vehicle at 6 months among patients with presumed inflammation-related low production; this occurred in 15% versus 5%, respectively. Ocular burning was reported in 17%. Other studies reported benefit after punctal occlusion and treatment success of 74%, 72%, and 67% in mild, moderate, and severe disease, respectively. After 1 full year of twice-daily use, some patients maintained benefit with once-daily dosing. A small retrospective study described improvement in signs, but not symptoms, after a median 23 (7–51) months of topical treatment, lasting a median of 20 (8–41) months. Cyclosporine may modify disease, but a 2019 Cochrane review of 30 randomized controlled trials involving 4,009 participants with average follow-up of 6 weeks to 12 months found inconsistent evidence for discomfort, staining, Schirmer findings, and TBUT. It suggested a possible increase in conjunctival goblet-cell numbers without evidence that mucus production improves; a large, long-term trial is needed. The FDA approved lifitegrast ophthalmic solution 5% in 2016 for signs and symptoms. Its precise therapeutic mechanism is unknown; proposed blockade of LFA-1 and ICAM-1 interaction could affect T-cell activation and migration. Published studies report improvement in signs and/or symptoms over 3 months; it appears safe over 12 months, but longer-term effects are unknown. Corticosteroids have been reported to improve irritation, fluorescein staining, and filamentary keratitis. One study reported improvement in irritation and corneal staining after 2-week nonpreserved topical corticosteroid pretreatment before punctal occlusion. A randomized prospective study of loteprednol etabonate 0.25% found symptom and conjunctival-hyperemia benefit over 2 weeks, but not improvement in surface staining, Schirmer results, or artificial-tear use; extending treatment to 4 weeks brought no further benefit or increase in adverse effects. Low-dose topical corticosteroids can be used infrequently for short courses of several weeks, with monitoring for increased intraocular pressure and cataract. Earlier reports suggested oral fatty acids might help, but a large masked prospective study found no benefit versus placebo over 12 months for moderate to severe dry eye (I-, Moderate, Discretionary). Other reports described some improvement with adjunctive omega-3 in blepharitis (I+, Moderate, Discretionary). Formulation variability limits high-quality supplement trials. The relationship of long-chain omega-3 supplementation to prostate-cancer risk remains unclear; two meta-analyses found no evidence that consumption changes that risk. FDA-approved varenicline nasal spray acts as a tear-production neuroactivator through nicotinic acetylcholine receptors and trigeminal signaling. A randomized phase-3 trial found it well tolerated, with a clinically meaningful effect on signs and symptoms. FDA-approved, preservative-free perfluorohexyloctane ophthalmic drops improved clinical findings versus hypotonic saline in a randomized multicenter double-masked phase-3 trial of meibomian-gland-related dry eye. Another randomized multicenter trial assigned 312 Chinese patients to perfluorohexyloctane or 0.6% NaCl drops four times daily for 2 months and reported significant improvement in meibomian-gland-related dry-eye signs and symptoms with perfluorohexyloctane. For aqueous deficiency, consider punctal occlusion when medical enhancement fails or is impractical, preferably once tear homeostasis is established. A Cochrane review found limited evidence from seven randomized trials for symptomatic benefit of silicone plugs in severe disease (I-, Insufficient, Discretionary). Silicone, collagen, and thermal labile polymer plugs are options; upper and lower duct occlusion produced similar lower-meniscus improvement. Appropriately sized silicone plugs can improve signs and symptoms and remain in place for years; the largest insertable plug should be used to reduce extrusion (I-, Insufficient, Discretionary). Position or shape can cause irritation, but silicone plugs can be removed for irritation or epiphora. One study found 56% retention after 2 years and reported canalicular stenosis at 2 years in 34% of patients whose plugs had been lost spontaneously. Patients benefiting from plugs that are lost may receive replacements or permanent punctal closure. Displaced plugs can obstruct the drainage system and cause infection, although surgical removal is rarely needed. Intracanalicular thermal labile polymer plugs avoid surface irritation but have been associated with epiphora, canaliculitis, dacryocystitis, and keratitis. Their use with concurrent inflammatory disease, including rosacea or allergic conjunctivitis, remains debated. Side shields and moisture chambers provide noninvasive options. Slow-release hydroxypropyl cellulose inserts sometimes help patients unable to instill artificial tears. Labial/buccal mucous membrane and minor salivary gland transplants have shown good results in SJS and ocular cicatricial pemphigoid.

document_sections.heading: Severe Dry Eye
document_sections.content: Severe disease may require therapies beyond those for mild and moderate disease. Thermal or laser cautery can permanently close puncta; laser is generally less effective for complete lasting closure and more expensive, while cautery is difficult to reverse. Usually perform a temporary-plug trial first to detect possible epiphora; silicone plugs are particularly useful. A staged cautery approach generally limits each session to no more than one punctum per eye. Limited tarsorrhaphy can reduce tear-film instability if other measures fail. Reports describe improved irritation and ocular-surface staining with autologous serum or autologous plasma rich in growth factors in Sjögren’s syndrome (I+, Insufficient, Strong) and GVHD. A systematic review reported symptom benefit from 20% autologous serum versus artificial tears over 2 weeks (I-, Insufficient, Discretionary). Allogeneic serum drops have been reported as an effective, safe alternative when repeated blood sampling is impossible. Filamentary keratitis can be managed by removing filaments with a moistened cotton-tip applicator, dry cellulose sponge, or forceps; topical N-acetylcysteine 10% can reduce mucinous-tear viscosity. Soft lenses can prevent filament recurrence but may be poorly tolerated in severe disease; use caution in neurotrophic keratopathy because of infection risk. A self-retaining or sutureless amniotic membrane should be considered in refractory cases, recognizing its short-lived effect. Rigid gas-permeable scleral lenses have been used successfully, although fitting difficulties, especially with cicatrization, expense, and ability or willingness to handle lenses can limit use. Selected patients may obtain relief from soft lenses, but infection risk, particularly with extended wear, must be considered. Oral medicines may help severe disease, especially combined ocular and oral dryness in Sjögren’s syndrome (I-, Moderate, Discretionary). FDA-approved cevimeline treats dry mouth in Sjögren’s syndrome and has been found to improve irritation and aqueous production; it may cause fewer systemic adverse effects than oral pilocarpine. These muscarinic-receptor-binding medicines stimulate glandular secretion, but most studies find greater oral than ocular benefit. Compared with placebo, pilocarpine 5 mg orally four times a day significantly improved focusing during reading and blurred vision in patients with Sjogren syndrome, without improving light sensitivity, ocular discomfort, or other dry-eye symptoms. Miosis may explain the visual improvement. Excessive sweating occurred in over 40% of pilocarpine recipients, and 2% withdrew because of sweating or other drug-related adverse effects.

document_sections.heading: Follow-up Evaluation
document_sections.content: Follow-up assesses therapeutic response to guide adjustment, checks for ocular-surface damage, and reassures patients. Its timing and extent depend on severity, treatment, and response; sterile corneal ulceration associated with dry eye may require daily review.

document_sections.heading: PROVIDER AND SETTING
document_sections.content: Diagnosis and management require broad medical expertise because systemic immune disease and medicines may contribute. Ophthalmologist evaluation is indicated with moderate or severe pain, failure to respond to treatment, corneal infiltration or ulceration, progressive conjunctival scarring, or loss of vision.

document_sections.heading: COUNSELING AND REFERRAL
document_sections.content: Explain chronicity, give specific treatment instructions, periodically reassess understanding and adherence, discuss benefits and possible complications again when needed, and jointly set realistic goals. Referral depends on severity and response. Timely referral to an ophthalmologist experienced with these conditions is recommended for treatment-resistant moderate to severe disease or suspected systemic disease. Consider internal-medicine or rheumatology referral for systemic immune dysfunction or a need for immunosuppression; an appropriate specialist should manage primary or secondary Sjögren’s syndrome and connective-tissue disease such as rheumatoid arthritis. Support groups and professional counseling may help selected patients cope. Severe dry eye increases contact-lens intolerance and related complications. Warn patients considering keratorefractive surgery, particularly LASIK, that symptoms may worsen; achieve effective dry-eye treatment before surgery. Uncontrolled dry eye syndrome contraindicates keratorefractive surgery.

document_sections.heading: SOCIOECONOMIC CONSIDERATIONS
document_sections.content: Reported dry-eye prevalence reaches 33% in Japan. U.S. Women’s Health Study and Physician’s Health Studies surveys reported physician-diagnosed disease or severe symptoms in 7.8% of women and 4.3% of men 50 and older. U.S. managed-care claims suggested diagnosed prevalence of 0.4% to 0.5% across all ages, highest among women and people 65 years and older; these data include only those seeking care and receiving diagnosis. A systematic review and meta-analysis considered U.S. incidence and prevalence of dry eye and meibomian gland disease uncertain because consistent validated definitions are needed; it reported dry-eye incidence of 3.5% in young adults and almost 8% above age 68, with no incidence studies for meibomian gland disease. Dry Eye Management Outcomes Simulation estimated approximately 1% prevalence in a typical managed-care population, with about 60% mild, 30% moderate, and 10% severe. It estimated care-seeking in about 20% of mild, 50% of moderate, and 100% of severe cases, implying approximately 0.4% of that population seeks care and receives a diagnosis. Studies associate dry eye with impaired reading and driving, daily, social and physical activities, work productivity, and quality of life. One study found reduced quality of life at every severity, with severe dry eye comparable in impact to moderate angina. Other studies found associations with anxiety, depression, pain, and activity limitations, including depression associated with symptoms regardless of treatment medicines. Vision-related quality of life is significantly affected through impaired reading. Economic evidence is limited but suggests substantial direct medical, direct nonmedical, indirect, and intangible costs. An online-database study involving 2171 patients estimated average annual treatment cost at $783 per patient, ranging from $757 to $809 in sensitivity analyses, and $3.84 billion for the U.S. health-care system; its societal estimates were $11,302 per patient annually and $55.4 billion overall. An English study reported over 6.4 million prescribed items in 2014 at a societal cost above £27 million. Three surveys found substantial health-care utilization, especially with Sjögren’s syndrome. Studies reported work interference averaging 184 to 200 days per year, absenteeism of 2 to 5 days per year, and productivity losses of more than $5,000 per patient per year for dry eye associated with Sjögren’s syndrome. Although largely palliative therapies can improve symptoms, few clinical studies have measured quality of life or economic outcomes, especially treatment cost. Prolonged topical treatment is costly, and insurance usually does not cover tear supplements.

document_sections.heading: ## APPENDIX 2. INTERNATIONAL STATISTICAL CLASSIFICATION OF DISEASES AND RELATED HEALTH PROBLEMS (ICD) CODES
document_sections.content: The appendix lists ICD-10 CM classifications for unspecified dry eye by lacrimal-gland laterality, keratoconjunctivitis sicca without specified Sjögren’s syndrome, Sjögren-associated sicca or keratoconjunctivitis, filamentary keratitis, exposure keratoconjunctivitis, and punctate keratitis. Applicable 7th characters must occupy the 7th position, using X to fill missing positions when needed. Where laterality is encoded, right corresponds to 1, left to 2, and bilateral to 3. If no bilateral code exists, code the left and right sides separately; use an unspecified code only when no other option applies.

document_sections.heading: ## APPENDIX 3. SJÖGREN’S SYNDROME
document_sections.content: Sjögren’s syndrome combines dry eye and dry mouth with systemic immune dysfunction. About 10% of patients with clinically significant dry eye have underlying Sjӧgren’s syndrome, which may be undiagnosed at ophthalmic presentation. Lymphocytic infiltration compromises lacrimal and salivary glands; systemic features can include arthralgia, myalgia, and fatigue. Primary disease may accompany thyroid dysfunction or autoimmune thyroiditis; secondary disease accompanies another distinct autoimmune disorder, such as rheumatoid arthritis, scleroderma, or systemic lupus erythematosus. Patients with either form should be comanaged with rheumatology because of possible systemic comorbidities. A Swedish epidemiologic study estimated prevalence at approximately 0.4%. A Greek study reported annual incidence of 5.3 per 100,000, prevalence of 92.8 cases per 100,000, and a female-to-male ratio of 20:1. A Slovenian study estimated primary-disease annual incidence at 3.9 per 100,000. Women receive the diagnosis much more often than men. Suspect the syndrome when a nonelderly woman develops intrinsic tear-production deficiency, especially if onset is rapid or deficiency marked. Identifying and treating systemic immune disease may reduce morbidity and may be lifesaving. Associated ocular immune manifestations include scleritis, sterile keratitis, and uveitis; vasculitic and lymphoproliferative disease can threaten life. Studies associate low C4 at diagnosis with higher lymphoma risk. The latest classification uses anti-SSA/Ro positivity and focal lymphocytic sialadenitis with ≥1 foci/4 mm2, scoring 3 each; ocular staining ≥5 or van Bijsterveld score ≥4, Schirmer ≤5 mm/5 minutes without anesthesia, and unstimulated saliva ≤0.1 ml/minute score 1 each. A total ≥4 in a person with suggestive findings meets the primary-disease criteria. Table A3-1 sets out the scoring, inclusion criteria, and exclusions. Sjögren’s Syndrome Foundation-supported expert guidance calls for assessment of discomfort, visual disturbance, relative aqueous and evaporative contributions, tear stability and osmolarity, lid-margin disease, and surface damage to guide severity-based care. It emphasizes education, tear supplementation and stabilization, inflammation control, and possible stimulation of secretion. A cited outcomes review noted a shortage of rigorous trials but considered lubricants, topical anti-inflammatory treatment, and tear conservation seemingly effective; oral secretagogues helped oral more than ocular dryness, while evidence did not strongly support hydroxychloroquine for dry eye. Another review found benefits for pilocarpine and cevimeline in sicca features, predominantly oral, and for cyclosporine in moderate or severe dry eye. Anti-tumor necrosis factor agents were not found effective, and evidence for rituximab efficacy was not strong.

document_sections.heading: ## APPENDIX 4. NEUROPATHIC OCULAR PAIN
document_sections.content: Neuropathic ocular pain (NOP) results from dysfunction of ocular-surface sensory nerves traveling through the nasociliary branch of cranial nerve V1 or of central neural pathways connecting the eye and brain. It may follow refractive or cataract surgery, infection including post-herpetic neuralgia, chronic surface inflammation or aqueous deficiency, or trauma including traumatic brain injury; it may also be idiopathic or coexist with migraine or fibromyalgia. Trigeminal-pathway hyperexcitability can produce spontaneous activity and chronic burning, stinging, or aching, often with photophobia or wind-related hyperalgesia. Diagnosis is challenging because NOP can coexist with aqueous deficiency and meibomian gland dysfunction, while environment and tear abnormalities may trigger corneal nociceptors. First assess the ocular surface and tear parameters for nociceptive causes, including deficiency, instability, inflammation, and erosions, and examine symptoms: in NOP, symptoms generally exceed visible findings. NPSI-Eye and OPAS can assess neuropathic characteristics. Persistent symptoms despite suitable treatment or resolution of tear and surface abnormalities provide another clue. When pain is present before testing, improvement after topical anesthetic suggests a nociceptive or peripheral neuropathic component; no improvement suggests a central or nonocular cause. Treatment depends on the site of dysfunction. Autologous serum tears can be used for peripheral NOP. For central pain or systemic comorbidity, oral pregabalin, gabapentin, duloxetine, amitriptyline, nortriptyline, or low-dose naltrexone have been used alone or together with variable success. With light sensitivity and headache, migraine-associated strategies such as transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation or periorbital botulinum toxin A injections may be considered. Periocular nerve blocks combining a corticosteroid and long-acting sodium channel blocker can be used for cutaneous allodynia or postsurgical pain. Approaches are often combined. Neuromodulators may require about 3 to 4 months at a therapeutic dose before pain decreases; counsel patients about delayed benefit. Anxiety, depression, and other mood disorders often coexist. Acupuncture, cognitive behavioral therapy, or hypnosis should be considered, and management warrants collaboration among ophthalmology, pain, neurology, and mental-health specialties.

document_sections.heading: ## APPENDIX 5. DIAGNOSTIC TESTS
document_sections.content: The appendix explains tests used to assess tear-film stability, ocular-surface disease, aqueous production and clearance, and osmolarity.

document_sections.heading: TEAR BREAK-UP TIME TEST
document_sections.content: Instill fluorescein in the inferior cul-de-sac, preferably using a strip moistened with sterile nonpreserved saline against inferior tarsal conjunctiva; combined fluorescein-anesthetic drops are unsuitable because anesthesia may alter results. After blinking, use a broad slit-lamp beam and cobalt blue filter. Measure the interval from the final blink to the first randomly located dark interruption of the stained precorneal film. Test before any drops or lid manipulation. Repeated breakup in one area may indicate localized anterior basement-membrane abnormality. A result less than 10 seconds is abnormal; rapid breakup occurs with aqueous deficiency and meibomian gland disease.

document_sections.heading: OCULAR SURFACE DYE STAINING
document_sections.content: Fluorescein, rose bengal, and lissamine green help assess ocular-surface abnormalities. Fluorescein penetrates epithelium where intercellular junctions are sufficiently disrupted; use a saline-moistened strip or 1% to 2% sodium fluorescein and examine with slit lamp and cobalt blue illumination. Staining may become clearer after about 2 minutes and with a yellow filter. Mild staining can occur in normal eyes, particularly in the morning; dry eye often produces exposure-zone punctate or blotchy staining, more readily seen on cornea than conjunctiva. Rose bengal may be applied with a moistened strip or 1% solution; advise patients that it can irritate, so topical anesthetic is typically used first. Leave saline against the strip for at least a minute before application. Rose bengal stains conjunctiva more intensely than cornea, highlighting cells lacking mucus coating and tear debris; a red-free filter can aid viewing. Lissamine green has a staining pattern resembling rose bengal with less irritation, but waiting 1 to 2 minutes reduces visibility; unlike fluorescein, it is not recommended to assess corneal epithelial disease. Diffuse corneal and conjunctival staining commonly accompanies viral keratoconjunctivitis or medicamentosa. Inferior corneal and bulbar conjunctival staining is typical of staphylococcal blepharitis, meibomian gland disease, lagophthalmos, or exposure; superior bulbar conjunctival staining is typical of superior limbic keratoconjunctivitis. Interpalpebral corneal and bulbar conjunctival staining commonly accompanies aqueous deficiency.

document_sections.heading: CORNEAL SENSATION TESTING
document_sections.content: Assess corneal sensation before placing drops, especially anesthetic. A fine point of cotton fibers or unflavored dental floss can provide a qualitative stimulus; sensation elicited by either indicates normal sensation. The amount of material required permits rough grading of neurotrophic keratopathy. A Cochet-Bonnet aesthesiometer measures sensation using an adjustable nylon filament: a lower number indicates less filament exposure and decreased sensation.

document_sections.heading: SCHIRMER TEST
document_sections.content: The Schirmer test estimates aqueous production but varies and should not independently establish dry eye. Place narrow filter paper in the inferior cul-de-sac, generally at the temporal one third, and measure wetting in millimeters, usually over 5 minutes. Testing may occur with or without anesthetic; Schirmer I conventionally omits anesthesia. The appendix describes the anesthetized test, termed Schirmer II or basic secretion testing, as reportedly more variable than testing without anesthesia. With anesthetic, less than 3 mm after 5 minutes strongly indicates aqueous tear deficient dry eye, whereas 3 to 10 mm may be equivocal. No absolute cutoff is established, but less than 10 mm over 5 minutes without anesthesia suggests abnormality; a basal secretion score of 5 to 10 mm is relatively insignificant. Schirmer I wetting less than 5.5 mm after 5 minutes is diagnostic of aqueous deficiency. Schirmer II assesses reflex secretion after stimulation of nasal mucosa with a cotton-tipped applicator; wetting less than 15 mm after 2 minutes is abnormal. If anesthetic is used, remove excess fluid before positioning the paper. A single low result may be nonspecific; repeatedly low results strongly suggest aqueous deficiency.

document_sections.heading: FLUORESCEIN DYE DISAPPEARANCE TEST/TEAR FUNCTION INDEX
document_sections.content: Fluorescein disappearance and tear function index assess surface tear clearance or turnover. After applying a measured amount of dye, compare residual color in the inferior meniscus and on a Schirmer strip against a standard scale. These methods assess aqueous production, tear volume, and drainage; cited work found stronger correlations with irritation severity and corneal fluorescein staining than for the Schirmer test.

document_sections.heading: TEAR OSMOLARITY TEST
document_sections.content: Osmolarity has long been regarded as relevant to dry eye, but point-of-care testing became more prominent after FDA clearance of TearLab in 2009. Published findings conflict: independent studies report strong correlation with severity and prediction of treatment response, while others criticize weak correlations with symptoms or other objective signs. At 312 mOsms/L, reported diagnostic sensitivity is 73% and specificity 92%. Comparators in cited data had sensitivity of 54% for corneal staining, 60% for conjunctival staining, and 61% for meibomian gland grading, or specificity of 45% for tear-film break-up time and 51% for Schirmer testing. These isolated values should be interpreted alongside symptoms and other findings. Change across time or conditions and clinical correlation may matter more than a single absolute result for diagnosis and monitoring. Recent studies report highly stable osmolarity in normal eyes and rapid loss of stability in dry eye with environmental changes. A large prospective study found higher, more variable readings in symptomatic people without significant surface or tear abnormalities than in controls, potentially suggesting osmolarity change precedes clinical findings. Multiple measurements over time are required for diagnosis in milder disease. Osmolarity may help rheumatologists or general practitioners unable to perform comprehensive external or slit-lamp examinations; more research and experience are needed to determine its clinical value.

document_sections.heading: MATRIX METALLOPROTEINASE-9 TEST
document_sections.content: A commercially available point-of-care matrix metalloproteinase-9 assay can assist diagnosis and, through its qualitative result, assessment of changes in disease state. It cannot distinguish dry eye from other inflammatory ocular-surface disorders, although it may help management.

document_sections.heading: ## LITERATURE SEARCHES FOR THIS PPP
document_sections.content: PubMed searches were performed on March 3, 2022, with focused updates on June 7, 2023. Filters addressed human English-language randomized controlled trials and systematic reviews, with a publication window beginning June 27, 2018. The panel analyzed 4,327 studies and included 50 in the guideline. Searches combining the disease with patient values or preferences returned no results. Economic-evaluation and treatment-cost searches found 66 studies, all 66 were supplied to the panel, and 1 was included. The study-identification diagram separately reports n = 4,327 records identified, n = 4,237 screened and assessed for eligibility, n = 4,187 excluded, and n =50 included.
